doc.title: Al Gallodoro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Oneonta, New York, December 28, 2005

title: Howard Voorhees teaches double and triple tonguing
summary: Voorhees taught him to practice slowly and shape the syllables.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Oh, Howard Voorhees, the man that got me into the Orpheum Theater, and the Forest Club.
Really? He showed you how to do that?

Yes. I’ll tell you what happened. Something went wrong with his embouchure and he couldn’t play trumpet but he could play the saxophone. So he took up the saxophone, practiced and practiced, and he adopted the double and triple tonguing on the saxophone.
I see. He used to do it on the brass instrument.

Yeah. So he showed me what to do. And he said practice slow. Don’t go for speed, the speed will come. Most everybody, they want to rush you know? Like play a passage and they’d rush. And I mean they flubbed, and they went on. I said, “Wait a minute, wait a minute. Stop right there. Correct that bar.” A half a dozen times, a hundred times.

Because if you keep going you’re going to make the same mistake every time. So that’s why he told me he said get the sound. Make sure that the “coo” sounds like a too. And he told me how to do this. And I practiced slow and I practiced slower. And that’s how it all came about.
That’s terrific. So we’re going to take another pause and we’ll bring JoAnn in here.
